PAGE 1

Some Basic Mathematical Models and Direction Field

This course is about differential equations which, at the most basic level, are simply equations containing derivatives.

Key Concept: A differential equation is an equation involving an unknown function and one or more of its derivatives. Solving it means finding all functions that satisfy the equality.

For example:

  • \( \frac{dy}{dx} = e^x \)
  • \( y' = x^2 + 2x - 5 \)
Yes, just basic calculus

So, you have seen differential equations before. But most are more complicated, for example:

Physical & Biological Models

\[ y'' + 3y' + y = 2 \]

Physical interpretation: Models the motion of a mass-spring-damper system with external force.

\[ \frac{dy}{dt} = ky \]

Model: Simple exponential growth (if \(k > 0\)) or decay (if \(k < 0\)).

Growth rate is proportional to size.

\[ \frac{dy}{dt} = k(L - y) \]

Model: Logistic growth (or decay), where \(L\) is the carrying capacity (environmental limit).

Rate proportional to \(L - y\).

PAGE 2

Verifying and Finding Solutions

For example, \( \frac{dy}{dx} = \cos x \) has a solution \( y(x) = \sin x + C \) because \( \frac{d}{dx}(\sin x + C) = \cos x \).

And \( y' = x^2 + 2x - 5 \) has \( y(x) = \frac{1}{3}x^3 + x^2 - 5x + C \) as its solution.

But what about \( \frac{dy}{dt} = k(L - y) \) or \( y'' + 3y' + y = 2 \)? Or even something as simple as \( y' = y \)?

We'll learn how to solve these in this course.

Guessing Solutions: The Equation \( y' = y \)

For now, notice we can sometimes guess the solution:

\( y' = y \) says that \( y \) is its own derivative.

So what is \( y \)? \( y = e^x, 2e^x, 3e^x, \dots \)

Generalize:

\[ y = C e^x \]

Family of Solutions: The constant \(C\) represents an arbitrary constant of integration. Each value of \(C\) gives a particular solution curve from the family of integral curves.

Graph: Family of Solutions

PAGE 3

Geometric Interpretation: Direction Fields

\( y' = y \) also says the slope of \( \overbrace{\text{the solution curve}}^{y(x)} \) is always equal to its \( y \) value.

Notice if I give you just the slopes you can “eyeball” the solution.

Concept Note: In a first-order differential equation \( y' = f(x,y) \), the derivative specifies the slope of the tangent line to the solution curve at every point \((x,y)\). By plotting small line segments with slope \( y' \) across a grid, one can visually trace trajectories without analytically solving the differential equation.

Back to \( y' = y \), let's try finding solution curves that way.

\( y' = y \) means:

  • on \( y = 0 \), \( y' = 0 \) (horizontal slope along the x-axis)
  • on \( y = 1 \), \( y' = 1 \) (slope of 1 along the line \( y=1 \))

This is called a Direction Field. We'll explore this further next time.
